title: How a Bengaluru Startup Turns Fruit Waste Into Ingredients That Replace Microplastics
excerpt: BacAlt Biosciences ferments agricultural waste into biopolymers that can replace the synthetic additives found in shampoos, toothpaste, and cleaning products.
body:
• BacAlt Biosciences, a Bengaluru-based startup, ferments fruit waste and crop residue into bacterial cellulose and poly-gamma glutamic acid — biopolymers that can replace petrochemical-based synthetic additives.
  • The company's product, ReRaw, is designed to replace up to five synthetic additives with a single biodegradable ingredient in personal care, oral care, and home care products.
  • BacAlt raised ₹18 crore (about $2 million) from Avaana Capital and Lubrizol InnoVentures, a strategic investor from the speciality chemicals industry.
  • A commercial launch planned for June 2026 has not been announced; no customer or revenue figures are public.

The shampoo, toothpaste, and floor cleaner in your home share something in common beyond the shelf they sit on. Each contains synthetic polymers — thickeners, stabilizers, and texture agents — that are overwhelmingly derived from petrochemicals. Many of those polymers end up in water systems as microplastics.

BacAlt Biosciences, a Bengaluru startup founded in 2023, is working to change that equation. The company ferments agricultural waste into biopolymers that can serve as drop-in replacements for synthetic additives, targeting a gap that has opened as regulators globally begin to restrict microplastics in consumer products.

From Waste to Biopolymers

The company's raw material is what most of the food industry throws away. BacAlt takes post-harvest crop waste and fruit waste from agro-industrial operations and feeds it through a fermentation process that produces two biopolymers: bacterial cellulose, which is produced by microbes rather than extracted from plants, and poly-gamma glutamic acid, a thickener and moisture-holding agent used widely in cosmetics and food science.

The cost challenge with biological alternatives has historically been the fermentation process itself. Industrial fermentation typically requires sterilized tanks — an energy-intensive step that adds cost, time, and points of failure if contamination occurs.

BacAlt says its process runs non-sterile, using high-throughput methods combined with waste feedstock to achieve what it describes as a multi-fold cost reduction compared to existing biopolymers at scale. This claim has not been independently verified.

The Product: ReRaw

The company has branded its primary offering as ReRaw, a blend of the two biopolymers. BacAlt says the blend can replace up to five synthetic additives with a single biodegradable ingredient, simplifying formulations for manufacturers while eliminating microplastic inputs.

The initial target markets are personal care, oral care, and home care products. The company has also named agrochemicals, nutraceuticals, pharmaceuticals, textiles, and wound care as future application areas.

"Recyclable packaging is not enough on its own. The formulations inside the bottle are where the microplastic problem actually sits."

— Shruti Kutmutia, CEO, BacAlt Biosciences

Funding and Strategic Backing

BacAlt raised ₹18 crore, approximately $2 million, in a round announced in September 2025. Avaana Capital led the investment, with participation from Lubrizol InnoVentures, the venture arm of American speciality chemicals company Lubrizol.

The Lubrizol investment is strategically significant. A corporate investor from the industry BacAlt intends to sell into brings distribution relationships and formulation expertise that a financial investor cannot. It also suggests the underlying technology has been evaluated by professionals who purchase speciality ingredients commercially.

The company, founded by CEO Shruti Kutmutia and co-founder Pranav Nair — both biotechnologists with backgrounds in microbiology and biopolymer fermentation — operates from Electronics City in Bengaluru and sells exclusively to other businesses.

Where It Stands

BacAlt had targeted June 2026 for its first commercial product launch from a pre-pilot facility in Bengaluru, with agrochemical and pharmaceutical markets to follow in 2027. That date has passed without a public announcement.

The company was shown at Bharat Innovates in Nice, France, in June 2026, where it described ReRaw and the partnerships it is seeking. No customer, order, or revenue figure has been made public. India's broader ambition to move from importing speciality ingredients to manufacturing and exporting them gives startups like BacAlt a tailwind — but the gap between a promising fermentation process and a commercially proven product remains wide.
